claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase FCC structure.
The starting alloy has a refined grain structure.
The starting alloy contains negligible pre-existing intergranular oxide precipitates.
Under oxidizing atmospheres, elevated-temperature degradation is primarily governed by enhanced grain-boundary diffusion.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion causes selective oxidation of Ti and Cr.
Selective oxidation produces nanoscale Ti- and Cr-rich oxide precipitates at FCC grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary oxides coalesce into a continuous intergranular network.
A continuous grain-boundary oxide network reduces intergranular cohesion and embrittles the alloy.
Reducing atmospheres suppress grain-boundary oxide formation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce thicker and more interconnected grain-boundary oxide layers than reducing or baseline exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce fatigue life relative to the untreated or inert-atmosphere baseline.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce hardness relative to the untreated or inert-atmosphere baseline.
Reducing exposure will retain mechanical integrity better than oxidizing exposure.
An inert-atmosphere exposure at the same temperature and duration will cause negligible oxide formation and no significant intergranular embrittlement.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 800–1000 °C because diffusion is appreciable in that range.
The mechanism may cease to govern degradation if other phase instabilities occur.
Exposure at 900 °C for 100 hours under oxidizing and hydrogen-containing reducing atmospheres provides a controlled comparison of the hypothesis.
Failure to observe greater grain-boundary oxidation together with greater mechanical degradation under oxidizing conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
